clinicalPearls: A rare, indolent mature B-cell malignancy that predominantly affects middle-aged and older men
Classically presents with pancytopenia, marked splenomegaly and often minimal lymphadenopathy
Monocytopenia is characteristic and predisposes to atypical and opportunistic infections
Circulating malignant cells show fine cytoplasmic projections, giving the hairy appearance on the blood film
Bone marrow is often difficult to aspirate (a dry tap) owing to marrow fibrosis
The BRAF V600E mutation is present in almost all cases of classic hairy cell leukaemia
It responds very well to purine analogue therapy, with durable remissions
reference.pathophysiology: Hairy cell leukaemia is a clonal proliferation of mature B lymphocytes with characteristic cytoplasmic projections. The near-universal BRAF V600E mutation activates the MAP kinase signalling pathway, driving proliferation and survival. The malignant cells infiltrate the bone marrow, spleen (particularly the red pulp) and liver, and induce a reticulin fibrosis that accounts for the frequent dry tap. Marrow infiltration and cytokine effects produce pancytopenia and the characteristic monocytopenia, which underlies the susceptibility to infection.
additionalDifferentials: Splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma
Other causes of pancytopenia with splenomegaly
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film review for characteristic cells
Flow cytometry showing a characteristic mature B-cell immunophenotype
Bone marrow trephine with immunohistochemistry when aspirate is unobtainable
Cross-sectional imaging to assess splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy
redFlags: Severe neutropenia with fever suggesting serious infection
Symptomatic massive splenomegaly or splenic rupture
Profound cytopenias causing bleeding or transfusion dependence
Features suggesting the more aggressive variant form
reference.prognosis: Classic hairy cell leukaemia has an excellent prognosis, with most patients achieving durable remission after purine analogue therapy and a near-normal life expectancy; relapses are usually retreatable.
pitfalls: Attributing pancytopenia to another marrow disorder and missing the diagnosis
Interpreting a dry tap as inadequate sampling rather than a clue to the disease
Overlooking the more treatment-resistant variant form
Failing to consider opportunistic infection in a monocytopenic patient
